product.title: Bengali 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Bengali: a pronunciation guide printed directly above every word in Bangla script, short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Bengali builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a full table of the Bangla script with its vowel signs, a guide to the unwritten vowel ô, the Sanskrit and Perso-Arabic words with a familiar ring, a summary of A1 verb forms across the three levels of politeness, and an English–Bengali glossary. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from consonants that carry a hidden vowel and sentences with no word for "is" to the -টা ending that turns a thing into the thing.

blocks.text: There is a language spoken by nearly three hundred million people. It gave Asia its first Nobel Prize in Literature, it supplies the national anthems of **two countries**, and it is the only language in the world whose speakers died to defend it — so that the UN now marks the day as International Mother Language Day. That language is Bengali, and outside South Asia hardly anyone teaches it.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote **আমার সোনার বাংলা**, now the national anthem of Bangladesh, and **জন গণ মন**, the national anthem of India — both in Bengali, both by the same man. And on 21 February 1952, students in Dhaka were shot dead for demanding that their language be recognized. That date is now International Mother Language Day, and the whole world marks it because of the language whose first page you have just opened.

The genuinely hard parts sit in three places, and this course won't pretend otherwise. First, **every Bengali consonant already carries a vowel inside it** — ক is not “k” but *kô*, and কম is read *kôm* even though no vowel sign is written at all. That hidden vowel sometimes sounds and sometimes vanishes, and guessing which is the work of week one. Second, **there are three ways to say “you”, each with its own verb forms** — তুই, তুমি, আপনি; choosing wrong is not just bad grammar but bad manners. Third, **the Bengali verb stands at the end of the sentence**, and prepositions become endings stuck onto the noun.

The good news far outweighs this. Bengali **has no grammatical gender at all** — no masculine and feminine as in Hindi, Arabic, or French, and the verb never changes because the speaker is a man or a woman. Better still, **the present tense drops “is/am/are” entirely**. আমি ছাত্র is literally “I student”, with no linking word. It feels odd for a week, then it feels like a gift: fewer words, and no *am/is/are* to choose between.

And there is a gift English speakers rarely hear about: **Bengali is a distant cousin of English**. Both descend from the same Indo-European ancestor, and the family resemblance still shows. নাম *nam* is *name*. দুই *dui* is *two*, তিন *tin* is *three*, সাত *sat* is *seven*, দশ *dôsh* is Latin *decem*, “ten”. On top of that sits a Persian-Arabic layer that English partly shares — বাজার is *bazaar*, কিতাব is *kitab*, “book” — and a Portuguese layer left by sailors: চাবি *chabi* “key” is Portuguese *chave*, বোতাম *botam* is *botão*, “button”.

Three things are deliberately different from the Bengali books already out there. First, **the pronunciation is printed right above each word**, not on a separate line — for Bengali this is a necessity, not a luxury, because the spelling hides vowels that are spoken and shows vowels that are dropped. Second, every line of dialogue has a **word-for-word translation** that shows the original word order, even when it sounds strange — that is exactly where the lesson lies. Third, every unit targets **one typical stumbling point for English speakers** and names it plainly.

Twenty units, one sitting of twenty to thirty minutes each. By the end you can introduce yourself, bargain at the market, order food, talk about yesterday, and say goodbye politely — in a language spoken from Kolkata to Dhaka, from Chittagong to the Bengali cafés of London's Brick Lane, New York, and Singapore. Say one Bengali sentence to a Bangladeshi you meet and watch what happens to their face. That is your first reward, and it comes much sooner than you think.

This course is designed for self-study, without a teacher, twenty to thirty minutes per sitting. One unit = one sitting. Don't do two units at once, however easy it feels — Bengali builds up in layers, and a unit done in a hurry will send you the bill in unit 13, when all the past-tense verb forms arrive at once.
Suggested order within a unit

items: **Read the title and the “by the end” list.** Those five lines are the unit's promise. If at the end you can do all five without looking, the unit is done.

**Read the dialogue aloud, twice.** Once looking at the pronunciation above the letters, once more covering it with your finger and trying to read the Bangla script directly. That second round is what teaches the script — not the alphabet chart.
**Only then read the translation.** Reversing this order is the most common mistake: if you read the meaning first, your eyes never truly look at the Bengali sentence.
**Pay attention to the literal line.** The small line under each sentence shows the original Bengali word order. That's where you learn to think in Bengali rather than translate from English.
**Do the exercises by hand, on paper.** Answering in your head feels faster and works far worse. The answer key is on the same page, so cover it with paper first.

blocks.title: Three tips that decide the result
items: **Don't wait until you know the whole script before starting unit 1.** The chart on the next two pages is for looking things up, not for memorizing. Bangla script sticks through rereading the dialogues, not through copying charts.

**Read aloud, even when you're alone.** Bengali distinguishes aspirated sounds (খ *kh*) from plain ones (ক *k*), and retroflex sounds (ট *T*) from dental ones (ত *t*). Those differences never get in through the eyes; only through the mouth and ears.
⚠️ **Use আপনি with everyone for your first three months.** তুমি and তুই sound warm between friends but rude to someone you've just met. Nobody ever took offense at being shown too much respect.

front.title: The Bangla script: letters that hang from a line

blocks.text: Look at the word বাংলা. There is a straight line running **along the top** of the letters, from left to right. It is called **মাত্রা** (*matra*), and it isn't decoration: it is what binds the letters into one word, just like the similar line in Devanagari. Writing Bangla means hanging letters from a line, not sitting them on one as with Latin letters.

Bangla is an **abugida**, not an alphabet. The difference is a single one, and it decides everything: every consonant **already carries a vowel inside it**. ক is not “k” but *kô*. ম is not “m” but *mô*. That's why কম is a complete word read *kôm*, even though no vowel sign is written — the first vowel rides on ক, while the one on ম is dropped because it ends the word.

To replace that hidden vowel with another one, you attach a sign called **কার** (*kar*). ক + া = কা *ka*. ক + ি = কি *ki*. ক + ু = কু *ku*. Eleven vowels have two shapes: an **independent** shape (used at the start of a word) and a **kar** shape (attached to a consonant). আম *am* uses the independent shape; কাম *kam* uses the kar shape.

blocks.title: Three surprises worth knowing from day one
items: ⚠️ **Three vowel signs are written on the LEFT but read after the consonant.** ি, ে, and ৈ stand in front of their consonant. কি is written “i-sign then ka” but read *ki*, not *ik*. It's not a misprint; that's how it's written. Two others — ো and ৌ — even wrap around the consonant from **both sides**: কো *ko*.

⚠️ **Two consonants that meet often fuse into a new shape** that looks nothing like its parents. ক + ষ becomes **ক্ষ** (*kkhô*), জ + ঞ becomes **জ্ঞ** (*ggô*), ত + র becomes **ত্র** (*trô*), ন + দ becomes **ন্দ** (*ndô*). These conjuncts are called যুক্তাক্ষর (*juktakshôr*), and there are hundreds, but only a dozen or so turn up often. This course prints the pronunciation above every word, so you don't need to hunt them down one by one.

**There are no capital and small letters.** Names, cities, and sentence starts are written with exactly the same letters. That's why **the pronunciation in this course never uses capitals for names or sentence starts** — capitals already have another job: marking retroflex sounds (T, Th, D, Dh, N, R). ঢাকা is written *Dhaka* — the capital D marks the retroflex sound, not the name of a city.

blocks.text: A sentence ends not with “.” but with a vertical stroke **।** called দাঁড়ি (*daⁿRi*). Question marks and exclamation marks are the same as in English. Even the digits have their own shapes — ০ ১ ২ ৩ ৪ ৫ ৬ ৭ ৮ ৯ — and they are still used on market prices, bus numbers, and house numbers in both Dhaka and Kolkata, so this course teaches them in unit 5.

One reassuring fact: Bengali and Assamese use practically the same script, and it is a close relative of Devanagari. If you ever learn Hindi, half the reading work is already done — the chart is laid out the same way, in the same order, with the same kar logic.

front.title: Sounds that fool you: ô, two e's, and the hiss

blocks.text: If there's one page in this course worth reading twice, it's this one. Not because the sounds are hard — most Bengali sounds are easy for English speakers — but because **Bengali spelling and Bengali sound often disagree**. The six points below explain nine out of ten beginner puzzles.
1. The hidden vowel অ is ô, not a

This is the biggest difference between Bengali and Hindi, and the most stubborn source of mistakes. The vowel stored inside every consonant **is not an a sound** but a **short, rounded o** — like *aw* in *law* or *o* in British *hot*, lips slightly rounded. কম = *kôm* (not *kam*), মন = *môn* (not *man*), বল = *bôl* (not *bal*). Anyone who has seen Hindi or Sanskrit words tends to read it as a; it's almost always wrong.

⚠️ This hidden vowel also **often disappears at the end of a word**. বল is written with two consonants but read *bôl*, one syllable, not *bô-lô*. Only the first one sounds. When it sounds and when it vanishes follows long rules; for now, just trust the pronunciation printed above every word.
2. এ has two sounds: é and è

The letter এ and its sign ে have **two different sounds**, and the spelling doesn't tell you which. Sometimes it's a closed **é**, like *ay* in *say* but without the glide — তেল *tél* (oil), মেয়ে *mèyé* (girl, second syllable). Sometimes it's an open **è**, like *e* in *bed* — এক *èk* (one), দেশ *dèsh* (country), দেখা *dèkha* (to see). That's why this course **always marks it**: é or è, never a plain e. Rarer still is **ê**, the *a* of *cat*, which you'll meet in words like ব্যাংক *bêngk* (bank).
3. শ, ষ, and স are almost always sh

Sanskrit distinguished three hissing letters; Bengali merges nearly all of them into one sound, **sh** as in *shoe*. শহর, ভাষা, and সব all start with sh. Only স keeps a plain **s** before certain consonants — সত্য *sôttô*, স্কুল *skul*, রাস্তা *rasta*. The good news: **picking the wrong one of the three will never cause a misunderstanding**, because native ears merge them too.
4. No native v, f, or z

ভ is **bh**, not v. ⚠️ Resist the urge to read *bh* as v, as many romanized Indian names tempt you to. ফ is an aspirated **ph** — never the *ph* of *phone* — though in everyday speech it often slides into f: কফি *kôphi · kôfi*. A z sound appears only in loanwords and usually turns into **j**. So *visa* becomes ভিসা *bhisa* and *zebra* becomes জেব্রা *jèbra*.
5. Retroflex and dental sounds

ট ঠ ড ঢ ণ ড় are made with **the tip of the tongue curled back toward the roof of the mouth** — this course writes them with capitals: T, Th, D, Dh, N, R. ত থ দ ধ ন are made with **the tongue touching the back of the teeth**, further forward than English t and d. ⚠️ The difference changes meaning: টাকা *Taka* is money, while তাকা *taka* means to look. English t and d sit between the two, so you only need to shift a little back or a little forward. And remember: *th* is t + breath, never the *th* of *think*.
6. Aspirated sounds — kh, gh, ch, jh, Th, Dh, th, dh, ph, bh

These ten letters are pronounced with **a puff of breath** following the sound. English already has the puff — the *p* in *pin* has it, the *p* in *spin* doesn't — but never uses it to tell words apart. To practice, hold your palm ten centimeters from your mouth. Say কাল *kal* — you feel nothing. Say খাল *khal* — your hand should feel the puff. ⚠️ The difference changes meaning, and often: কাল *kal* = yesterday/tomorrow, খাল *khal* = canal; দাম *dam* = price, ধাম *dham* = holy place; পল *pôl* = moment, ফল *phôl* = fruit.

blocks.title: Four words to test your ear
items: **কাকা** *kaka* — uncle. Two plain k sounds, no puff at all.
**খাখা** — not a word, but say it anyway: two puffs in a row. Feel the difference from the word above.
**টাকা** *Taka* — money (the currency of Bangladesh). First sound retroflex, second sound plain.
**তাড়াতাড়ি** *taRataRi* — quickly. Dental, retroflex flap, dental, retroflex flap. If this word comes out smoothly, your ear is ready.

front.title: Bengali words with a familiar ring

blocks.text: Bengali is an Indo-European language — a distant cousin of English, Latin, and Greek. On top of that old family tie, it drank from three wells: **Sanskrit**, **Persian-Arabic**, and **Portuguese**. Some of these words will ring a bell straight away; others are simply the core vocabulary you'll meet again and again. Read the list slowly — it gives you a head start before unit 1 even begins.
From Sanskrit — the oldest layer
Even the numbers are family

Bengali numbers come down from the same Indo-European roots as English, Latin, and Greek ones. Once you see the links, one to ten stop feeling foreign: **এক** *èk* — Sanskrit **eka** · **দুই** *dui* — **two**, *duo* · **তিন** *tin* — **three**, *tri*- · **চার** *char* — Latin *quattuor*, *quarter* · **পাঁচ** *paⁿch* — Greek **penta**gon · **ছয়** *chhôy* — **six**, *hexa*- · **সাত** *sat* — **seven**, *sept*- · **আট** *aT* — **eight**, *octo*- · **নয়** *nôy* — **nine**, *nova*- · **দশ** *dôsh* — **ten**, *deca*-.
From Persian and Arabic — the second layer
From Portuguese — the third layer, left by sailors

Portuguese ships called at Bengal in the 1500s and left words behind. **জানালা** *janala* is “window” — Portuguese *janela*; **গির্জা** *girja* is “church” — *igreja*; **আনারস** *anarôsh* is “pineapple” — *ananás*; **চাবি** *chabi* is “key” — *chave*; **বোতাম** *botam* is “button” — *botão*; **সাগু** *sagu* is *sago*; **কুলি** *kuli* is “porter”, the word English borrowed as *coolie*.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Fifteen everyday words with a twist
items: **চিন্তা** *chinta* = **thought, worry**. চিন্তা করো না means “don't worry”. For love, the word is **ভালোবাসা** *bhalobasha*.
**বিচার** *bichar* = **judgment, trial**. To talk, the word is **বলা** *bôla* or **কথা বলা** *kôtha bôla*.
**সংসার** *sôngshar* = **household, family life** — a warm word, used about home and family.
**পরীক্ষা** *pôriksha* = **exam**, not just a check. পরীক্ষা দেওয়া means to sit an exam.
**ভাগ্য** *bhaggô* = **fate, luck** — which can be good or bad.
**নদী** *nôdi* = **river**. Don't mix it up with নাড়ি *naRi*, “pulse” — similar, but not the same word.
**দেশ** *dèsh* = **country, homeland** — and also “home region”. A village is **গ্রাম** *gram*.
**বাবু** *babu* = **sir, gentleman** — a respectful title, not “baby”.
**বাতাস** *batash* = **wind, breeze** — the everyday word; হাওয়া is its Perso-Arabic twin.
**খেয়াল** *khèyal* = **attention, mind**. খেয়াল রেখো means “take care of yourself”.
**উকিল** *ukil* = **lawyer**.
**ইস্ত্রি** *istri* = **iron** (for clothes). A wife is **স্ত্রী** *stri* — one extra i at the front turns a life partner into a household appliance.
**জল** *jôl* = **water**, an everyday word in Kolkata, not a poetic one. In Bangladesh people mostly say **পানি** *pani*.
**অর্থ** *ôrthô* = **meaning** and also **money**. Both are right; context decides.
**হালকা** *halka* = **light** (not heavy). Often used about food and work.

blocks.text: One last note about this list. Sanskrit loanwords in Bengali are called **তৎসম** (*tôtsômô*) and usually feel more formal; the everyday word is often different. But many of them are perfectly everyday: সূর্য *surjô* is the normal word for the sun, and for the earth people really do say পৃথিবী, just as in the list. So these words aren't just historical decoration — you will actually use them.

back.title: Nouns: the -টা ending, plurals, and role markers

blocks.text: Bengali never changes the shape of a noun; it **adds endings**. One noun can carry three endings at once, always in the same order: **noun + definite marker + plural + role marker**. বই → বই**গুলো**র (of those books). This page sums up every ending used in this course.

blocks.text: Place words that need the possessive ending

blocks.title: ⚠️ The four most common mistakes
items: **Stacking এটা and -টা.** The right form is **এই বইটা**, not *এটা বইটা*.
**Using -টা for people.** For people use **-জন** (with numbers) or **-টি** (refined): তিনজন ছাত্র, মেয়েটি.
**Marking the plural twice.** তিনটা বই is enough; *তিনটা বইগুলো* is wrong — a number already makes it plural.
**Forgetting the possessive before a place word.** The right form is **বাড়ির সামনে**, not *বাড়ি সামনে* — think “in front **of** the house”.

blocks.title: Verb patterns to learn as a whole
items: **… তে চাই** — want to: আমি যেতে চাই (I want to go).
**… তে পারি** — can: আমি যেতে পারি (I can go).
**…কে … তে হবে** — must: আমাকে যেতে হবে (I must go). ⚠️ The person takes the -কে ending.
**… তে ইচ্ছে করছে** — feel like: আমার ঘুমাতে ইচ্ছে করছে (I feel like sleeping). ⚠️ The person takes the possessive form.
**… ভালো লাগে** — like: আমার গান ভালো লাগে (I like songs). ⚠️ The person takes the possessive form.

blocks.text: One to a hundred

⚠️ Above a thousand, Bengali doesn't count in millions but in **লাখ** *lakh* (a hundred thousand) and **কোটি** *koTi* (ten million). One million is **দশ লাখ**, ten million is **এক কোটি**. Big numbers are grouped the same way in writing: ১০,০০,০০০ = 10,00,000 = 1,000,000.
Telling the time

⚠️ **সাড়ে + a number means half past that hour.** সাড়ে তিনটা = 3:30, just like “half past three”. But সাড়ে is never used for 1:30 and 2:30 — each of those has its own word, দেড়টা and আড়াইটা, much like “one and a half”.

blocks.text: **Dates** use ordinal forms: ১ **পয়লা**, ২ **দোসরা**, ৩ **তেসরা**, ৪ **চৌঠা**; after that add **-ই** to the number (পাঁচই, সাতই, চৌদ্দই), and **-এ** from the 20th on (বাইশে, পঁচিশে). The Western months are the familiar English names in Bengali script: জানুয়ারি, ফেব্রুয়ারি, মার্চ, এপ্রিল, মে, জুন, জুলাই, আগস্ট, সেপ্টেম্বর, অক্টোবর, নভেম্বর, ডিসেম্বর.

The Bengali calendar has twelve months of its own — **বৈশাখ, জ্যৈষ্ঠ, আষাঢ়, শ্রাবণ, ভাদ্র, আশ্বিন, কার্তিক, অগ্রহায়ণ, পৌষ, মাঘ, ফাল্গুন, চৈত্র** — and its New Year, **পহেলা বৈশাখ**, falls on April 14.

Words that point to people, places, and times

blocks.title: A pattern that saves a lot of memorizing
items: Look down the columns above: **ক-** always asks, **এ-** is always near, **ও-** is always far, **স-/ত-** always points back to something already mentioned. Once you see the pattern, these twenty-odd words stop feeling like twenty separate words.
**A question word stays where the answer would go**, not at the front of the sentence as in English. আপনি **কোথায়** থাকেন? — literally “you where live?”

⚠️ **কি and কী.** কি (short) slips inside the sentence and isn't translated; কী (long) means “what”. In casual writing people often spell them the same, but native ears still tell them apart by their position.

blocks.text: Every word from the vocabulary lists of all twenty units, in English alphabetical order. Pronunciation key: **ô** = short rounded o, as in *law* (said short); **é** = closed e, like *ay* in *say* without the glide; **è** = open e, as in *bed*; **ê** = a as in *cat*; **capital T Th D Dh R** = retroflex sounds; **ⁿ** = nasal vowel; **ch** = as in *church*, **chh** = the same with a puff of air; **sh** = as in *shoe*.

blocks.text: This course stops here, but the language doesn't. The twenty units you've just finished cover **the full A1 level of the CEFR**: you can introduce yourself, handle everyday needs, ask and answer questions about familiar things, and talk about the past and your plans in simple sentences. What comes next isn't more rules to memorize — it's **flying hours**.
Four habits that make the biggest difference

items: **Read one sign a day.** Bangla script sticks through short, frequent repetition, not long sessions. Shop signs, headlines, and food packaging are the lightest and most repetitive practice material there is.

**Listen to something you don't understand, every day, for twenty minutes.** Radio news, podcasts, songs. Don't stop to translate. Your ear builds sound patterns on its own, below conscious awareness.
**Write three sentences a day.** About the weather, your lunch, what you saw. Mistakes don't matter; what matters is the habit of building your own sentences instead of repeating other people's.

**Find one person to talk to every week.** This matters most and gets put off most. Start with **আমি একটু একটু বাংলা বলি** and let the conversation run; almost every Bengali speaker slows down once they know you're learning.

blocks.title: Material worth seeking out
items: **Songs:** রবীন্দ্রসঙ্গীত (Rabindra Sangeet) for clear, slow lyrics; নজরুলগীতি for energy; modern Bangladeshi bands for everyday language.
**Films:** the work of সত্যজিৎ রায় (Satyajit Ray) — clear dialogue, unhurried pace; modern Bangladeshi films for the Dhaka accent.

**Reading:** at this stage children's stories and comics are more useful than newspapers, because the sentences are short and repetitive. **ঠাকুরমার ঝুলি** — a classic collection of Bengali folk tales — is a delightful place to start.

**Conversation:** there are Bengali communities in London, New York, Toronto, Sydney, and almost every big city in the world. People from Bangladesh and West Bengal alike will welcome any foreigner who tries.

blocks.text: One last thing, and it isn't a polite closing line. Bengali is a language whose speakers once walked into gunfire to defend the right to speak it, and the whole world marks that date every year as International Mother Language Day. They know very well how rarely foreigners take the trouble to learn it. Your first sentences — halting, even wrong — will be met with a warmth that may leave you a little awkward. Just accept it; it isn't a verdict on your skill, it's a thank-you for making the effort.
**শুভকামনা** *shubhôkamôna* — good luck. **ভালো থাকবেন** — take care. **আর আবার দেখা হবে** — and see you again.
